o: From index i you may jump to the nearest j > i with nums[j] >= nums[i] (all in-between strictly smaller), or to the nearest j > i with nums[j] < nums[i] (all in-between >= nums[i]). Each arrival at j costs costs[j]; minimize total cost to reach n-1. Since both rules point to the *nearest* qualifying index, each node has at most two outgoing edges, computable with monotonic stacks. Because all edges go forward, a left-to-right DP relaxation suffices — no Dijkstra needed despite the tag.
k: Edges from i: nextGreaterOrEqual(i) and nextSmaller(i), both found with monotonic stacks in O(n).
All edges go rightward, so indices form a DAG and one forward pass relaxes all distances.
dist[0] = 0 (you do not pay costs[0]); answer is dist[n-1].

a.i: Scan right-to-left maintaining a monotonic stack to record, for each i, the nearest index to the right with a greater-or-equal value and the nearest with a smaller value. Then process indices left to right, relaxing dist[j] = min(dist[j], dist[i] + costs[j]) along both outgoing edges. Reachability of n-1 is guaranteed since one of the two targets always exists for i < n-1.
s: Build ng[i] = nearest j > i with nums[j] >= nums[i] using a stack of indices with values < nums[i] popped away.
Build nl[i] = nearest j > i with nums[j] < nums[i] symmetrically.
For i in 0..n-1, relax dist[ng[i]] and dist[nl[i]] with dist[i] + costs[target]. Return dist[n-1].
a.t: O(n) — two stack builds plus one relaxation pass.
a.sp: O(n) — stacks, edge arrays, distance array.

a.i: Construct the same two-edges-per-node graph and run Dijkstra from node 0 with edge weight costs[j] into j. This is more general (works even if edges were bidirectional or arbitrary) at the cost of a log factor, and is what many contestants write first given the Shortest Path tag.
s: Build adjacency lists from the ng/nl arrays.
Run Dijkstra with a min-heap seeded with (0, 0).
Pop the cheapest node; skip stale entries; relax its two neighbors.
a.t: O(n log n) — Dijkstra with a binary heap over at most 2n edges.

w: In an interview, lead with the observation that 'nearest qualifying index' bounds out-degree to 2, then note the DAG structure makes plain DP optimal; mention Dijkstra as the fallback. Pitfalls: paying costs[0] (should not), mixing up strict/non-strict comparisons between the two stack builds, and integer overflow of summed costs (use 64-bit). Follow-up: reconstruct the cheapest path, or allow jumps in both directions.
